source: Windsor, P.A. 2014. 'HS for Train the Trainers' -- ACIAR/USYD Mekong Livestock Research project resource (mekonglivestock.wordpress.com)
text: This trainer-level background note on Haemorrhagic Septicaemia (HS) describes it as an acute, often fatal bacterial disease (Pasteurella multocida, serotype B2 in Asia) mainly of cattle and buffalo, though also reported in pigs, deer, horses, donkeys, elephants, and yaks. Affected animals can die within 24 hours with no warning signs, though most show fever (41-42 degrees C), respiratory distress, nasal discharge, increased salivation, and swelling in the neck spreading to the brisket over 2-3 days; buffalo are more susceptible than cattle, and young animals more susceptible than adults in both species. Mortality can reach up to 100%, mostly in older calves or young adults, and recovery is rare unless treated very early. Risk increases with high humidity at the start of the rainy season, free-range management, high buffalo density, poor husbandry, and draught animals under work stress; in Cambodia specifically, outbreaks are more likely where farmer disease-prevention knowledge is weak and where cattle trading/movement is high (the note cites roughly 17% of village cattle being bought and sold annually in Cambodia). Prevention requires strategic twice-yearly vaccination of all cattle and buffalo over 3 months old (initial two doses 1-3 months apart), and general eradication is considered unfeasible, so ongoing biosecurity (quarantine, movement control, traceability, and disinfection) is the realistic control approach.
